title: Duty according to nature (18.41–18.48)
hook: your own path, done badly, beats someone else's done well
carry: your own dharma, imperfect, beats another's, perfect

segments.voice: Yesterday, three kinds of knowledge, action and doer, and dirghasutri, the long-threaded procrastinator. Today, a hard and important passage.

Five minutes of scrolling, and there they are: a dozen lives that look better. Someone's startup, someone's travel, someone's calm morning routine. It's easy to start living their life in your head, copying their plan, their job, their whole personality. The Gita has a line about this. It said it once already, in chapter three, and here in chapter eighteen it comes again, almost word for word: your own dharma, even done imperfectly, is better than someone else's, done perfectly. But the verses around it need care.
screen: `A DOZEN BETTER-LOOKING LIVES.` → `COPYING SOMEONE ELSE'S PATH.` → `YOUR OWN, EVEN IMPERFECT.`

segments.voice: Verses forty-one to forty-four describe the four varnas, the classes of ancient Indian society: brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras. Their work, Krishna says, is divided by the qualities born of their nature. Calm, self-control, learning and faith for brahmins. Courage, skill and generosity for kshatriyas, Arjuna's class of warriors. Farming, cattle and trade for vaishyas. Service for shudras. This is where honesty matters. You met a classmate's version of this question on day ninety-five; here it is in the Gita itself. These verses have been used to support caste as a hierarchy fixed by birth, and people were deeply hurt by it. The reformer B. R. Ambedkar criticized the Gita sharply for this. Some modern Hindu teachers read varna as temperament and calling rather than birth, pointing to chapter four, where Krishna says the four were made by quality and action. Hindus still disagree about this, and the disagreement is real. Then verse forty-five turns to the heart of the passage: a person who is devoted to their own work reaches perfection. Verse forty-six: by worshiping, through their own work, the one from whom all beings come, a person reaches perfection. In this verse, work itself becomes worship. Verse forty-seven: better your own dharma, even imperfect, than another's, even done well. Verse forty-eight adds: don't abandon the work that's yours, even if it has flaws. Every undertaking is wrapped in some fault, the way fire is wrapped in smoke. Whatever one makes of the varna verses, these last four say: find what's truly yours to do, and do it, smoke and all.
screen: `FOUR VARNAS, BY QUALITY AND WORK.` · `USED TO DEFEND CASTE BY BIRTH.` · `YOUR WORK CAN BE WORSHIP.` · `EVERY FIRE HAS SOME SMOKE.` · then, large: `DUTY ACCORDING TO NATURE.`

segments.voice: Think of a life you've envied lately, let it come fully into view, then gently set it down. Now think of the work actually in front of you, your family, your job, your studies, your one small patch of the world, and notice its imperfections, the smoke. Then notice the fire, the part that's truly yours, that no one else could do quite the same way, and rest there.
Svadharma, one's own dharma. Gita eighteen: your own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's done well; your own work can be worship.
Your line: your own dharma, imperfect, beats another's, perfect. Your work can be worship. That's day two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Some Hindus understand svadharma as the duties that belong to their own life and stage of life, and offer their daily work as worship; how the Gita's varna verses relate to birth-based caste is still debated among Hindus.

original.note: Sanskrit: svadharma, one's own (sva) dharma: the duty and path that belong to you; Gita 3.35 and 18.47.

what it means: it names the social order of its time, and teaches that your own path, done imperfectly, is better than borrowing another's.

what a scholar hears: 18.41–18.44 assign duties to the four varnas 'by gunas born of nature'; 18.47 repeats 3.35 'shreyan svadharmo vigunah'; readings of varna as birth or temperament (cf. 4.13) remain contested.

options: The Gita says your own dharma, even imperfect, beats another's done perfectly.
